title: The Physician's Road to La Moneda: Medicine, the Ballot Box, and the Eleventh of September
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Notary's Son on the Move

stops.name: Santiago, born on Avenida España
stops.date_confidence: Date attested. Birthplace contested but not evenly: en.wikipedia, es.wikipedia and the Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional all give Santiago, es.wikipedia naming the house at Avenida España 615; the widely repeated Valparaiso version is a secondary tradition with no source of comparable standing. A minority of accounts give 26 July for the date. Coordinates are the Nominatim placement of Avenida España, Santiago, not a verified street number.
stops.campa: A son is born to the lawyer Salvador Allende Castro and Laura Gossens Uribe in a house on Avenida España, at the western edge of Santiago. The family is professional gentry with a radical streak: notaries, lawyers, and a grandfather, Ramon Allende Padin, who wore the Masonic apron two generations before the boy is given it. Valparaiso will claim the birth anyway, for the next century, because Valparaiso is where the Allendes belong and where the family's dead are counted. They name the child for his father.
suggested_refs: The house at Avenida España 615, Santiago, named by the Spanish-language record as the birthplace
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica de Salvador Allende Gossens (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Tacna, the childhood in administered territory
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the move and the reason (the father's postings); the month is unrecorded and defaulted to January. The family's years in Tacna are given as roughly 1909 to 1916.
stops.campa: The father's work carries the household north to Tacna, a province Chile holds and administers while the treaty that would settle it stays unwritten. Peruvian families keep their language and their saints under a Chilean flag, and the plebiscite promised for the province is put off decade after decade. Allende Castro works as a lawyer and notary among people whose nationality is a pending question. The son is a year old when they arrive and eight when they leave. The promised plebiscite is still unheld on the day the family goes south.
suggested_refs: The Chilean administrative offices of Tacna, where Allende Castro practised as lawyer and notary

stops.name: Iquique, the nitrate coast
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the relocation, year approximate, month unrecorded and defaulted to January. The claim that the nitrate zone founded his politics is his own later account, and biographers treat it as retrospective.
stops.campa: The family comes down the coast to Iquique, the port that ships the nitrate out and the wages in. The oficinas run inland from the sea, their workers paid in tokens good only at the company store, and the pampa delivers its saltpetre to a city of consulates and imported pianos. The boy is eight. He will say later that the distance between the two Iquiques was the beginning of everything he became. He says it while running for president, and his biographers file the claim as a retrospective one.
suggested_refs: The nitrate oficinas of the Tarapaca pampa and the company-token economy of the 1910s

stops.name: Santiago, the Instituto Nacional
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the school; month unrecorded, defaulted to January. Coordinates from the Nominatim entry for the Instituto Nacional José Miguel Carrera, Arturo Prat, Santiago.
stops.campa: For a season the postings put him in the capital, in the oldest public secondary school in the country, where the republic has been manufacturing its lawyers, its presidents and its opponents since before there was a republic. He is one boy in a corridor of them, ten years old. The schooling of these years is peripatetic and never finished in one place: four cities in six years, the far north, the capital, the deep south, none of them home for longer than the length of a posting. Whether any of it took is not a question the school records answer.
suggested_refs: The Instituto Nacional José Miguel Carrera, calle Arturo Prat, Santiago

stops.name: Valdivia, the liceo in the south
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the school; the year is given as 1919 with attendance running into the early 1920s. Month unrecorded, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: The household moves again, this time into the rain, and he is enrolled at the Liceo de Valdivia among the sons of German colonists and of smallholders from the river country. Valdivia is breweries, shipyards and timber, wet nine months of the year, two thousand kilometres from the desert schoolroom he has just left. He is eleven, and by the time he finishes school he will have been a pupil in the far north, the capital and the deep south of a country that is mostly coastline. Nothing else is recorded of the year but the enrolment.
suggested_refs: The Liceo de Valdivia and the river-port city of the 1920s

stops.name: Valparaiso, the shoemaker Juan De Marchi
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the school years (roughly 1922 to 1924) and for the friendship with De Marchi; month unrecorded, defaulted to January. The single-conversation origin story told about the friendship is biographical shorthand. Coordinates from the Nominatim entry for the Liceo Eduardo de la Barra, Avenida Colon, Valparaiso.
stops.campa: He finishes his humanities at the Liceo Eduardo de la Barra, and in the port outside it he finds his real teacher: Juan De Marchi, an Italian anarchist who mends shoes and lends books. It is the first political education he chooses for himself rather than inherits. The boy sits on the bench in the workshop while the old man talks about Bakunin, about the state, about who owns the wharf and who works it, and hands him pamphlets his father would not keep in the house. The shoemaker goes on mending while he talks.
suggested_refs: Juan De Marchi's shoemaking workshop in Valparaiso, and the Liceo Eduardo de la Barra
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Viña del Mar, a year in the cavalry
stops.date_confidence: The fact of one year of voluntary cavalry service before university is attested; every detail of it is disputed. bcn.cl gives the Regimiento Coraceros of Viña del Mar in 1926; en.wikipedia gives the Cuirassier Regiment of Tacna in 1925; es.wikipedia gives the Regimiento de Lanceros of Tacna, completed by 1924. The stop is placed at Viña del Mar on the strength of the official Congress biography, and the coordinates are the city centre, not a located barracks.
stops.campa: Before the university he does his year of voluntary military service in a cavalry regiment: riding, shooting, the care of horses, the manners of officers at table. It is the only formal military training he will ever have. He keeps the taste for it, and the uniform photographs, and an ease with soldiers that will let him believe, at the worst possible moment, that he knows what the officer corps is. The record cannot agree on which regiment, which city, or even which year.
suggested_refs: The Regimiento Coraceros barracks at Viña del Mar, named by the Congress biography as the site of his service
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Santiago, the Facultad de Medicina
stops.date_confidence: Entry in 1926 attested; month unrecorded, defaulted to January. The vice-presidency of the FECh in 1929 is reconstruction rather than document. Graduation year is unsettled: en.wikipedia says he retook his sixth year and graduated at 23, bcn.cl gives the title in 1932, and both agree the thesis is dated 1933. The 1931 expulsion is attested, but the sources name no place of relegation, only 'the north'. Coordinates are the Facultad de Medicina at Avenida Independencia 1027 per Nominatim.
stops.campa: He enters medicine at the Universidad de Chile and finds the second half of his education in the corridor rather than the lecture hall: a Marxist reading group, the presidency of the medical students' centre, street work against the dictatorship of Carlos Ibanez del Campo, a cell in a police station more than once. In 1931 the university expels him and the government relegates him north. He comes back, retakes the year, and finishes with a thesis on mental hygiene and delinquency, arguing that criminals are produced by conditions rather than born.
suggested_refs: The thesis 'Higiene mental y delincuencia', Universidad de Chile, dated 1933
The Facultad de Medicina, Avenida Independencia 1027, Santiago
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Valparaiso, the lodge Progreso No. 4
stops.date_confidence: The lodge is agreed: Progreso No. 4 of Valparaiso, under the Gran Logia de Chile. The year is not: en.wikipedia gives 1928, es.wikipedia gives 1935. Placed here at the earlier date to keep the family thread with his grandfather intact, and flagged as unresolved; no Gran Logia de Chile record was reached to settle it. Month unrecorded, defaulted to January. Coordinates are the Valparaiso city pin.
stops.campa: He is initiated into Freemasonry in the lodge Progreso No. 4 of Valparaiso, taking up a family trade: his grandfather Ramon Allende Padin had been a Mason and a physician before him, which in nineteenth-century Chile was nearly the same profession twice. The lodge gives him a second network alongside the party, one that crosses class and political line, and a formal habit of oath-taking. He remains a Mason for the rest of his life. The year is disputed: one record gives 1928, another 1935, and no lodge register was reached to settle it.
suggested_refs: Lodge Progreso No. 4, Valparaiso, under the Gran Logia de Chile

stops.name: Valparaiso, the morgue of the Hospital Van Buren
stops.date_confidence: Attested: en.wikipedia gives 1932 for the start of practice as physician and anatomo-pathologist in the morgue of the Van Buren hospital; bcn.cl confirms service in the Asistencia Publica of Valparaiso from 1932 to 1936. Month unrecorded, defaulted to January. Coordinates from the Nominatim entry for the Hospital Carlos Van Buren, calle San Ignacio 725.
stops.campa: No hospital in the country will hire a doctor with his arrest record, so he takes the work nobody wants and becomes an anatomo-pathologist in the morgue of the Van Buren, opening the bodies of the port poor. Tuberculosis, malnutrition, industrial accident, the diseases of bad water and worse housing, over and over, in men of thirty. He keeps count. What he will argue from a platform for the next forty years he is reading here first, off a table, in the order the bodies come in. He holds the post in the Asistencia Publica of Valparaiso from 1932 to 1936.
suggested_refs: The Hospital Carlos Van Buren and the Asistencia Publica of Valparaiso, 1932-1936
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Valparaiso, founding the Socialist Party in the port
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the year and the role. The Partido Socialista de Chile was founded nationally in April 1933; the day of the Valparaiso branch's constitution is not given in the sources reached and is defaulted to the first of the month.
stops.campa: A year after the twelve-day Socialist Republic collapses, the surviving groups assemble themselves into a party, and Allende builds its branch in Valparaiso. Marmaduke Grove, Eugenio Matte and Oscar Schnake lead it nationally. The new party declares itself Marxist and refuses Moscow's discipline, a position that will shape Chilean politics for forty years and keep the Socialists and the Communists arguing inside every alliance they ever make. He is twenty-five, a morgue physician with a party card he helped print.
suggested_refs: The founding documents of the Partido Socialista de Chile, April 1933
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Caldera, relegated to the coast of Atacama
stops.date_confidence: The relegation of 1935 is attested; the place is not. en.wikipedia gives Caldera on the Atacama coast and calls it his second relegation; es.wikipedia gives Calama in the Loa desert, six months, under the second government of Arturo Alessandri. The two towns are some 500 km apart. Placed at Caldera and flagged unresolved. Month unrecorded, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: The government removes him from Valparaiso and sets him down in a small northern port, several months of internal exile with the sea on one side and the desert on the other. Relegation is the republic's polite instrument: no trial, no sentence, only a distance. He reads, he treats whoever comes to him, he writes to the party. It is the second time the state has moved him for his politics and he is not yet thirty. Which town it was is disputed: the record offers Caldera on the coast and Calama in the desert, five hundred kilometres apart.
suggested_refs: The Atacama coastal towns used for relegation under the Alessandri government

stops.name: Valparaiso and Quillota, elected deputy
stops.date_confidence: Attested by bcn.cl: Deputy for the Sixth District, Valparaiso and Quillota, 1937-1941. The polling day is not given in the sources reached and is defaulted to March 1937. The variant 'Valparaiso-Aconcagua' sometimes attached to this seat is a conflation with his 1961-1969 Senate district and is not used here.
stops.campa: The port sends its morgue doctor to Congress. He takes the Sixth District, Valparaiso and Quillota, for the Popular Front, and arrives in the chamber with a physician's brief: sanitary legislation, maternity provision, hours and conditions in the docks and the mines. He is twenty-eight and one of the youngest deputies in the house. From this seat he will hold elected office almost without a break for thirty-six years: deputy, minister, senator, president of the Senate, president of the republic.
suggested_refs: The Sixth Departmental District of Valparaiso and Quillota, 1937-1941
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Santiago, Minister of Health under Aguirre Cerda
stops.date_confidence: Start date 28 September 1939 confirmed by bcn.cl and en.wikipedia (es.wikipedia gives a divergent 28 August 1939). The closing date is contested: bcn.cl gives 7 April 1942, en.wikipedia and es.wikipedia give 2 April 1942. Coordinates are an approximate downtown Santiago placement; the ministry's building of that era was not confirmed.
stops.campa: Pedro Aguirre Cerda gives him the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Social Assistance, and for two and a half years he runs the state's medicine instead of describing it. Typhus and venereal-disease campaigns, milk for mothers and infants, industrial safety rules, the beginnings of a national health service that will take another decade to legislate. Chile at the time buries a fifth of its children before their first year. That figure is what he works from and what he is still quoting thirty years later. He is thirty-one when he takes the office; the sources disagree by five days about the date he leaves it.
suggested_refs: The Ministry of Health, Welfare and Social Assistance under the Popular Front, 1939-1942
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Santiago, La realidad medico-social chilena
stops.date_confidence: Attested as his principal authored monograph, published 1939 in the ministry period; month unrecorded and defaulted to January. Coordinates are the canonical Santiago pin, since no publication address was confirmed.
stops.campa: He publishes the book that is his one substantial work of authorship: mortality tables, tuberculosis rates, wages set against the price of bread, housing measured in cubic metres of air per sleeping body, the whole assembled into an argument that disease in Chile is a distribution problem wearing a clinical mask. It is a minister's report written as an indictment. Nothing in it is rhetorical; the numbers do the accusing. The title is as flat as a ledger entry: La realidad medico-social chilena, the Chilean medical and social reality.
suggested_refs: Salvador Allende, 'La realidad medico-social chilena' (Santiago, 1939)
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Santiago, marriage to Hortensia Bussi
stops.date_confidence: The year 1940 is attested by bcn.cl; the day is contested. es.wikipedia's article on Hortensia Bussi gives 17 March 1940, its article on Allende gives 16 September 1940. The meeting is attested by es.wikipedia: they met in Santiago on the night of 24 January 1939, during the Chillan earthquake, not afterwards. The ceremony's venue is unidentified; coordinates are the canonical Santiago pin.
stops.campa: He marries Hortensia Bussi Soto, a teacher and librarian he met in Santiago on the night the Chillan earthquake shook the city and killed thousands to the south. She is called Tencha for the rest of a life that will hold three daughters, a presidency, a coup, and twenty years of exile carrying her husband's papers from capital to capital. The record cannot settle the wedding day: one page gives 17 March 1940, another 16 September of the same year.
suggested_refs: The Chillan earthquake of 24 January 1939, on whose night they met in Santiago
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Ex Congreso Nacional, the senator and the Ley Maldita
stops.date_confidence: Senate service from 15 May 1945 attested by bcn.cl, initially for the southern provinces of Valdivia, Llanquihue, Chiloe, Aisen and Magallanes. His opposition to the 1948 Ley de Defensa Permanente de la Democracia is reconstruction from the secondary record rather than a roll call reached in this pass. Coordinates from the Nominatim entry for the Palacio del Ex Congreso Nacional.
stops.campa: He enters the Senate for the far south, Valdivia to Magallanes, provinces reached by ship and measured in fjords, and he will hold a Senate seat for the next twenty-four years. In 1948 Gabriel Gonzalez Videla, elected with communist votes, outlaws the Communist Party and ships its militants to a camp in the Atacama at Pisagua. Allende opposes it; the alliance he assembles twenty-one years later is built largely out of the people that law tried to erase. The statute is titled the Permanent Defence of Democracy. The chamber calls it the Accursed Law.
suggested_refs: The Ley de Defensa Permanente de la Democracia, 1948, and the Pisagua camp
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Santiago, the first two campaigns
stops.date_confidence: Both results attested: about 5.4 per cent in 1952, and roughly 28.5 to 28.9 per cent against Jorge Alessandri's approximately 31.6 per cent on 4 September 1958. The stop is dated to the 1952 election and covers both. Coordinates are the canonical Santiago pin.
stops.campa: He runs for president the first time with his own party divided against him and a small Socialist and Communist coalition behind him, and takes five per cent. Six years later, as candidate of the Frente de Accion Popular, he comes within about thirty thousand votes of the presidency of Chile. Nothing about him has changed between the two results except the arithmetic, and the arithmetic is what the Chilean right reads in 1958. Washington reads the same table. He is fifty years old when he loses it.
suggested_refs: The Frente de Accion Popular (FRAP), the 1958 and 1964 coalition
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Santiago, the 1964 campaign and the American money
stops.date_confidence: Attested: roughly 38.6 to 38.9 per cent to Eduardo Frei Montalva's 55.6 to 56.1 per cent on 4 September 1964. The Church Committee's later estimate of about three million dollars in covert United States support to Frei's campaign is attested in the same sources; the figure is an estimate, not an accounting.
stops.campa: Against Eduardo Frei Montalva and the Christian Democrats he loses by nearly twenty points, and the campaign that beats him is partly paid for from Washington: posters, radio, women's committees, leaflets showing Soviet tanks in Santiago streets, some three million dollars of it by the Senate's later reckoning. He raises his own vote by ten points and loses worse than before. It is the third defeat, and he is fifty-six years old. The Senate committee that names the figure will not publish it for another eleven years, and calls it an estimate rather than an accounting.
suggested_refs: United States Senate Select Committee (Church Committee), 'Covert Action in Chile 1963-1973' (1975)
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Ex Congreso Nacional, President of the Senate
stops.date_confidence: Attested by bcn.cl: President of the Senate, 27 December 1966 to 15 May 1969. Coordinates from the Nominatim entry for the Palacio del Ex Congreso Nacional.
stops.campa: The chamber elects him its president, and for two and a half years the leading Marxist in Chile presides over the upper house of a liberal republic, keeps its order, rules on its procedure, and receives its foreign guests. It is the constitutional argument of his whole life made into an office. He travels as Senate president, to Cuba and to Europe; he brings home survivors and refugees. He holds the chair from 27 December 1966 to 15 May 1969, and gives it up fifteen months before the election he finally wins.
suggested_refs: The presidency of the Chilean Senate, 27 December 1966 to 15 May 1969
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Santiago, Unidad Popular assembled
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the composition of the coalition (Socialists, Communists, Radicals, MAPU, Accion Popular Independiente) and for the internal bargaining that produced his candidacy; the month is unrecorded and defaulted to January.
stops.campa: Socialists, Communists, Radicals, MAPU and the small parties assemble into Unidad Popular, and after weeks of bargaining the coalition settles on the candidate who has already lost three times, in part because none of the others can be agreed. His own party gives him its nomination without enthusiasm. The programme they hand him is a full one: nationalisation of copper, agrarian reform, banking in state hands, all of it by legislation, all of it inside a constitution nobody proposes to suspend.
suggested_refs: The Programa Basico de Gobierno de la Unidad Popular, 1969

stops.name: Santiago, the plurality of 4 September
stops.date_confidence: Attested: 36.61 per cent and 1,070,334 votes against Jorge Alessandri's 35.27 per cent and Radomiro Tomic's 28.11 per cent, with no absolute majority, which sends the decision to Congress.
stops.campa: One million and seventy thousand Chileans vote for him, thirty-six per cent and change, thirty-nine thousand votes ahead of Jorge Alessandri, with Radomiro Tomic third. Nobody has a majority, so the constitution hands the choice to Congress, which by custom confirms whoever came first. Between the count and the vote in Congress lie fifty days. In those fifty days the currency will run, the banks will empty, an army commander will be shot in the street, and Chile will find out what its custom is worth.
suggested_refs: The Chilean presidential election of 4 September 1970 and its vote table

stops.name: Santiago, the balcony of the student federation
stops.date_confidence: The victory speech from the balcony of the Federation of Chilean Students building is attested and dated to September 1970 by the Marxists Internet Archive; the exact night and the building's street address were not confirmed in this pass, and the coordinates are the canonical Santiago pin.
stops.campa: He speaks to the crowd from the balcony of the student federation on the Alameda, in the small hours, to people who have been waiting in the street since the count began. He tells them the win is theirs and not his, that he is one man with the ordinary quantity of faults, and that what is coming will be built rather than destroyed. Below him the Alameda is full from side to side. In the residential districts to the east, people are already queuing at the banks.
stops.quote: I am only a man, with every shortcoming and weakness that any man has.
stops.quote_source: Salvador Allende, victory speech from the balcony of the Federation of Chilean Students building, Santiago, September 1970 (Marxists Internet Archive)
suggested_refs: The Federation of Chilean Students building on the Alameda, Santiago
sources: Marxists Internet Archive, Salvador Allende archive, victory speech, September 1970

stops.name: Santiago, the killing of Rene Schneider
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Schneider was shot resisting a kidnapping on 22 October 1970 and died of his wounds on 25 October. The exact intersection is not named in the sources reached and the coordinates are an approximate eastern-Santiago placement. The 16 October 1970 CIA cable is a declassified document held by the National Security Archive.
stops.campa: General Rene Schneider holds the doctrine that the army obeys the constitution and does not choose presidents, which makes him the last obstacle between the election and a coup. Men trying to abduct him shoot him through the car window on his way to work; he dies three days later. Six days before that, a cable from Langley to the Santiago station had put the policy in a single sentence. The kidnapping was meant to produce a crisis the army would resolve. It produces a martyr, and Congress confirms Allende two days later.
stops.quote: It is firm and continuing policy that Allende be overthrown by a coup.
stops.quote_source: CIA Headquarters operating guidance cable to the Santiago Station, 16 October 1970, declassified; National Security Archive Electronic Briefing Book No. 8
suggested_refs: The declassified Track II / Project FUBELT files, National Security Archive Electronic Briefing Book No. 8
sources: National Security Archive, Electronic Briefing Book No. 8

stops.name: Ex Congreso Nacional, confirmed by 153 votes
stops.date_confidence: Attested and exact: 153 votes to 35 for Alessandri with seven blanks, 24 October 1970, per es.wikipedia's article on the 1970 presidential election and bcn.cl. The Statute of Constitutional Guarantees was the Christian Democrats' price. Coordinates from the Nominatim entry for the Palacio del Ex Congreso Nacional.
stops.campa: Congress meets with Schneider three days in his grave and confirms him: one hundred and fifty-three votes to thirty-five, seven blank. The price is a Statute of Constitutional Guarantees, written into the constitution at Christian Democrat insistence, binding the incoming government to press freedom, to the parties, to the schools, and to the army's institutional autonomy. He signs it. His own left calls the signature a surrender; he calls it the terms on which the thing can be done at all.
suggested_refs: The Estatuto de Garantias Constitucionales, October 1970
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Palacio de La Moneda, the sash
stops.date_confidence: Attested by bcn.cl and en.wikipedia. The description of him as the first self-identified Marxist elected head of state in a competitive liberal democracy is the standard formula and is imprecise, since no fixed global definition governs it. The dismissal of the diplomat Miguel Serrano on Allende's election is carried on Serrano's own atlas file.
stops.campa: He takes the sash in the palace of La Moneda, a building put up as a colonial mint, and becomes the head of state of a country that has just been persuaded to elect a Marxist without shooting anybody. The government has a programme and a plurality of thirty-six per cent, and it does not control Congress. The diplomatic service is turned over; among those stripped of a post is the ambassador and occultist Miguel Serrano, dismissed from state service, who will spend the rest of his life writing against everything this morning stands for.
suggested_refs: The Palacio de La Moneda, built 1784-1805 as the colonial mint
sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)
serrano.journey.json (atlas), 1970 dismissal from the diplomatic service

stops.name: Tomas Moro, the house in Las Condes
stops.date_confidence: Attested as the presidential residence of the Allende years and as a target of the air force on 11 September 1973 (es.wikipedia, 'Golpe de Estado en Chile de 1973'). The month of occupancy is unrecorded and defaulted to January 1971. Coordinates from the Nominatim entry for the Casa presidencial de Tomas Moro, Avenida Tomas Moro 200, Las Condes.
stops.campa: The presidential household settles in Las Condes, in a house on Avenida Tomas Moro with a garden, a swimming pool, and walls that fill with pictures: Chilean painters, pre-Columbian pieces, gifts from delegations. He also keeps the flat on Guardia Vieja in Providencia. A president who calls himself a workers' president lives comfortably and does not pretend otherwise, dresses well, likes whisky and good tailoring. On the last morning the Hawker Hunters will bomb this house too, after they have finished with the palace.
suggested_refs: The Casa presidencial de Tomas Moro, Avenida Tomas Moro 200, Las Condes, bombed 11 September 1973
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Golpe de Estado en Chile de 1973'

stops.name: Ex Congreso Nacional, the first annual message
stops.date_confidence: The text is verbatim from the Marxists Internet Archive page filed under a September 1970 date; that filing is a cataloguing artifact. The speech self-dates to the First Annual Message to the National Congress, 21 May 1971: it speaks of six months of government, of copper coming under Chilean ownership later that year, and of the April 1972 UNCTAD conference to come. He was not president in September 1970.
stops.campa: Six months into the government he goes to Congress for the annual message and lays out what he claims is a second road: a transition to socialism made by ballot, statute and purchase order rather than by insurrection, the first of its kind attempted anywhere. He grants the difference from Russia in 1917 openly. His opponents in the chamber hear a man announcing the end of the republic; his own left hears a man refusing to arm it. Both are listening to the same sentence. The archive that keeps the text files it under September 1970, a year before he was president.
stops.quote: The Chilean people are achieving political power without having used arms. They are taking the road of social emancipation having had to fight only the limitations of a liberal democracy and not a despotic or dictatorial regime.
stops.quote_source: Salvador Allende, First Annual Message to the National Congress, Santiago, 21 May 1971 (Marxists Internet Archive)
suggested_refs: The Primer Mensaje al Congreso Pleno, 21 May 1971, section 'Violence'
sources: Marxists Internet Archive, Salvador Allende archive, First Annual Message to the National Congress

stops.name: Rancagua, the Day of National Dignity
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Congress approved Law 17,450 unanimously and Allende promulgated it on 11 July 1971 as the Day of National Dignity, nationalising the Anaconda and Kennecott properties at Chuquicamata, El Salvador and El Teniente. The venue within Rancagua, plaza or stadium, was not confirmed against a transcript in this pass.
stops.campa: Every party in Congress, including the ones that will spend the next two years trying to destroy him, votes for the copper law without a single vote against. Anaconda and Kennecott lose Chuquicamata, El Salvador and El Teniente, and the compensation is reduced by what the state calculates as excess profit already taken, which is to say to nothing. He signs it in Rancagua, at the gate of El Teniente, and names the day the Day of National Dignity. Kennecott begins attaching Chilean copper cargoes in European ports.
suggested_refs: Law 17,450 of 11 July 1971 and the El Teniente mine above Rancagua
sources: standard histories of the Chilean copper nationalisation

stops.name: Palacio de La Moneda, Fidel Castro's twenty-four days
stops.date_confidence: Attested by es.wikipedia's article on the visit: 10 November to 4 December 1971, the longest visit by a foreign head of government to Chile to that date. The farewell speech acknowledging the severity of the class conflict was given at the Estadio Nacional on 2 December, not at La Moneda; this stop is the hosting locus only.
stops.campa: Fidel Castro arrives for what is announced as a short state visit and stays twenty-four days, going from Chuquicamata to Tierra del Fuego, into mines, schools and union halls, talking wherever he stops. Received at La Moneda by a president who has taken power by counting votes, he says plainly at the end that a revolution made at the ballot box has no army of its own. The right reads the visit as proof of what Chile has become. Allende keeps the rifle Castro gives him, engraved to his friend and comrade-in-arms.
suggested_refs: The engraved rifle given by Fidel Castro to Salvador Allende
Castro's farewell speech at the Estadio Nacional, 2 December 1971
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Visita de Fidel Castro a Chile'

stops.name: Santiago, the strike of the truck owners
stops.date_confidence: The strike began in the early hours of 9 October 1972 (es.wikipedia, 'Gobierno de Salvador Allende'); its length is usually given as twenty-four to twenty-six days depending on the endpoint chosen. The Cybersyn telex network's use during it is attested by en.wikipedia's Project Cybersyn article, quoting Gustavo Silva on moving resources into the city with about two hundred trucks.
stops.campa: The lorry owners stop the country, and a country shaped like a ribbon four thousand kilometres long can be strangled by a few thousand parked trucks. Shops empty; the opposition unions and professional guilds join; the strike is later shown to have been partly financed from abroad. The government answers with a telex network built for other purposes, finding which trucks are still running and where the fuel is, and moves the capital's supplies with about two hundred vehicles. Then he puts generals in the cabinet.
suggested_refs: The October 1972 paro de camioneros and the civic-military cabinet that followed

stops.name: United Nations, New York, against the corporations
stops.date_confidence: Attested: address to the United Nations General Assembly, 4 December 1972. The text is held by the Marxists Internet Archive and the speech is among the fifty preserved by the Fundacion Salvador Allende's speech archive.
stops.campa: He stands at the green marble rostrum in New York and tells the General Assembly that his country is under attack by companies rather than armies: ITT, which tried to prevent his taking office, and the copper firms now attaching Chilean cargoes in foreign ports. He describes corporations larger than the budgets of the states that host them, answerable to no parliament anywhere. The hall gives him a long ovation. He is in New York for a day. From the airport the aircraft turns east, for Moscow.
stops.quote: The corporations are global organizations that do not depend on any state and whose activities are not controlled by, nor are they accountable to any parliament or any other institution representative of the collective interest.
stops.quote_source: Salvador Allende, address to the United Nations General Assembly, 4 December 1972 (Marxists Internet Archive)
suggested_refs: The General Assembly Hall, United Nations Headquarters, New York
The audiovisual record of the 4 December 1972 address, Fundacion Salvador Allende, '50 discursos'
sources: Marxists Internet Archive, Salvador Allende archive, address to the UN General Assembly

stops.name: The Kremlin, Moscow, asking for money
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The Moscow visit in December 1972, on the same journey as the United Nations address, and the disappointing outcome are carried by the general historical record and the research dossier; no primary record of the meetings was reached in this pass, and the venue within the Kremlin complex is unconfirmed.
stops.campa: From New York he goes to Moscow to ask for emergency credit, and the Soviet leadership does the arithmetic in front of him: Chile is very far away, its government has no control of its army, and Cuba already costs a million dollars a day. He is given courtesies, some credits, and nothing near what he came for. The socialist camp declines to buy a second Latin American dependency. He flies home to a treasury with less than a month of foreign exchange in it.
suggested_refs: Soviet economic assistance decisions on Chile, December 1972
sources: research dossier, Moscow visit of December 1972 (unverified in this pass)

stops.name: Providencia, the Opsroom on Avenida Santa Maria
stops.date_confidence: The room, its design under CORFO with Stafford Beer's team, and Beer's account of Allende's response are documented in Cybersyn scholarship. The 30 December 1972 visit date could not be confirmed against any source reached. Coordinates follow es.wikipedia's 'Proyecto Synco', which places the Opsroom in a building on Avenida Santa Maria near the Philips offices, resolved by Nominatim to Avenida Santa Maria 760.
stops.campa: In a building on Avenida Santa Maria, north of the river, seven fibreglass chairs stand in a hexagon under screens: the operations room of Project Synco, built with the British cybernetician Stafford Beer to run a national economy by telex. Beer shows the president the diagram of the viable system and points to the level marked for the people. Allende taps it and says that one goes at the top. The screens are not live. The slides behind them are drawn by hand, one frame at a time, and the room never governs anything.
suggested_refs: The Opsroom of Proyecto Synco, Avenida Santa Maria, Santiago
Eden Medina's archival reconstruction of Project Cybersyn

stops.name: Santiago, the March elections
stops.date_confidence: Attested: parliamentary elections of 4 March 1973, with Unidad Popular at about 44 per cent (44.03 per cent and 63 deputies per es.wikipedia's article on the election, 43.5 per cent in its article on the government) against the opposition CODE's 55.70 per cent and 87 deputies. The often-quoted 43.4 per cent sits at the low end of the range.
stops.campa: After two years of shortages, queues, inflation and strikes, the government goes to a parliamentary election expecting to be punished and instead raises its vote to about forty-four per cent, above what it won in 1970. The opposition takes both chambers but falls well short of the two-thirds it needed to remove the president by constitutional means. The arithmetic closes the legal exit; there is now no lawful route to a change of government, and the men who want one know it by the evening of the count. The next presidential election falls due in 1976.
suggested_refs: The Chilean parliamentary elections of 4 March 1973

stops.name: Santiago, the Tanquetazo
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the date, the leader and the outcome; Lieutenant Colonel Roberto Souper's armoured regiment attacked the government quarter on 29 June 1973 and General Carlos Prats led its suppression. The tank column's route was not confirmed street by street and the coordinates are an approximate downtown placement.
stops.campa: An armoured regiment under Lieutenant Colonel Roberto Souper drives into the government quarter and shells the palace and the defence ministry for a morning. Twenty-two people are killed. General Carlos Prats, commander-in-chief and constitutionalist, walks out and takes the surrender of the tanks in person, on foot, in front of the guns. What the morning settles is which officers are willing to move and which are not, and the answer is now on file with both sides. Among the dead is an Argentine cameraman whose camera goes on running while the soldier who kills him takes aim.
suggested_refs: Leonardo Henrichsen's film of his own killing, Santiago, 29 June 1973

stops.name: Ex Congreso Nacional, the Chamber declares the breakdown
stops.date_confidence: The date and the phrase 'grave quebrantamiento del orden constitucional y legal' are confirmed by es.wikipedia's article on the coup, with the text carried on Wikisource and officially noticed on 23 August. The often-quoted 81 to 47 tally could not be confirmed in any source reached and is omitted here.
stops.campa: The opposition majority in the Chamber of Deputies votes an accord declaring a grave breakdown of the constitutional and legal order and calls on the ministers who are serving officers to put an end to it. It impeaches nobody, removes nobody, and authorises nothing; it is an address, not a law. Three weeks later the men who take the palace will quote it in their first communiques as the country's invitation. Allende answers that the chamber has asked the armed forces to break their oath.
suggested_refs: The Acuerdo de la Camara de Diputados of 22 August 1973, text on Wikisource
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Golpe de Estado en Chile de 1973'
Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, reseña biográfica (bcn.cl)

stops.name: Santiago, Prats resigns and Pinochet takes the army
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the sequence and the date: Prats resigned on 23 August 1973 after right-wing demonstrations including a protest by generals' wives outside his house, and Allende appointed Augusto Pinochet in his place, nineteen days before the coup.
stops.campa: The wives of his fellow generals demonstrate outside Carlos Prats's house and the officer corps declines to defend him, so Prats resigns as commander-in-chief. Within the year he will be killed by a car bomb in Buenos Aires, on the orders of the man he is about to recommend. He recommends his own deputy as a loyal constitutionalist, and Allende signs the appointment of Augusto Pinochet, who has served the government through the copper nationalisation and the tank revolt without a mark against him. The date is 23 August 1973.
suggested_refs: The assassination of Carlos Prats and Sofia Cuthbert, Buenos Aires, 30 September 1974

stops.name: Valparaiso, the fleet comes back at dawn
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the fleet, which had sailed for joint exercises, reappeared off Valparaiso around dawn and the navy seized the port and city before the other services moved (es.wikipedia, 'Golpe de Estado en Chile de 1973').
stops.campa: The fleet had put to sea for exercises with the United States navy the day before. Before dawn it is back off Valparaiso, and marines take the port, the radio stations and the streets of the city where he went to school, worked the morgue, built his party and was first elected. The telephone call reaches the president at Tomas Moro a little after six: the navy has risen. He puts on a jacket, takes a helmet and the rifle, and goes down to the palace instead of to the airport.
suggested_refs: The Valparaiso naval command and the port seizure of 11 September 1973
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Golpe de Estado en Chile de 1973'

stops.name: Palacio de La Moneda, Radio Magallanes
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the final address went out over Radio Magallanes at about 10:15 a.m., the last station still transmitting; the tank and artillery assault on the palace began about 10:30 and the Hawker Hunters struck between about 11:30 a.m. and 12:08 p.m. (es.wikipedia). The English text quoted is Yoshie Furuhashi's translation, held by the Marxists Internet Archive.
stops.campa: The commanders of the four services demand his resignation and offer him an aircraft. He refuses both, and at a quarter past ten he speaks into the microphone of the last radio station still transmitting, over the noise of the aircraft coming in. He tells them he will pay with his life for the loyalty of the people, that he is not resigning, that they should not let themselves be cut down but should not be humiliated either. Fifteen minutes later the tanks open fire, and an hour after that the jets come in low over the Alameda.
stops.quote: Go forward knowing that, sooner rather than later, the great avenues will open again where free men will walk to build a better society.
stops.quote_source: Salvador Allende, 'Last Words to the Nation', Radio Magallanes, Santiago, 11 September 1973, trans. Yoshie Furuhashi (Marxists Internet Archive)
suggested_refs: The Radio Magallanes transmission of 11 September 1973, preserved in the Fundacion Salvador Allende's speech archive
sources: Marxists Internet Archive, 'Last Words to the Nation'
es.wikipedia.org, 'Golpe de Estado en Chile de 1973'

stops.name: Palacio de La Moneda, the Salon Independencia
stops.date_confidence: Attested by en.wikipedia's 'Death of Salvador Allende': at about 1:50 p.m. he ordered the defenders to surrender, shook hands with them in a line, then walked to the Salon Independencia; the physician Patricio Guijon turned back and saw him shoot himself. The body reached the Hospital Militar at about 17:30. The 2011 forensic panel found the injuries consistent with suicide by a rifle set to automatic fire.
stops.campa: Infantry are inside the building and the upper floor is burning when he orders the defenders out. He shakes their hands one by one along the line, tells them to go down and not to be killed for him, and walks back alone into the Salon Independencia with the rifle Fidel Castro gave him. The physician Patricio Guijon turns back for a gas mask and sees him do it. The soldiers carry the body out wrapped in a Bolivian blanket, and it reaches the Hospital Militar at about half past five in the afternoon.
stops.quote: The people must defend themselves, but they must not sacrifice themselves.
stops.quote_source: Salvador Allende, 'Last Words to the Nation', Radio Magallanes, Santiago, 11 September 1973, trans. Yoshie Furuhashi (Marxists Internet Archive)
suggested_refs: The Salon Independencia of La Moneda, where the original Acta de la Independencia de Chile also burned
The AK-pattern rifle inscribed 'To my friend and comrade-in-arms, Fidel Castro'
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Golpe de Estado en Chile de 1973'

stops.name: Cementerio Santa Ines, Viña del Mar, the grave with another family's name
stops.date_confidence: Attested by es.wikipedia's 'Fundacion Salvador Allende': buried on 12 September 1973, clandestinely, in the tomb of the Grove family at the Cementerio de Santa Ines, Viña del Mar. Coordinates from Nominatim for the cemetery. The Nixon telephone transcript is National Security Archive EBB No. 437, Document 7, read as page images; the wording follows the scan, including the trailing 'though'.
stops.campa: The junta will not permit a funeral, so the body goes into the ground the next day at Santa Ines in Viña del Mar, in the tomb of the Grove family, under a stone that does not carry his name. His widow is allowed to be present with almost nobody else. Five days later, in Washington, the president of the United States and his national security adviser discuss on the telephone how the thing is going to be played, and settle on a version in which nobody's hand shows.
stops.quote: Well we didn't - as you know - our hand doesn't show on this one though.
stops.quote_source: Richard Nixon to Henry Kissinger, telephone conversation, 16 September 1973, 11:50 a.m.; National Security Archive Electronic Briefing Book No. 437, Document 7
suggested_refs: The Grove family tomb, Cementerio de Santa Ines, Viña del Mar
Kissinger-Nixon telcon of 16 September 1973, National Security Archive EBB No. 437
sources: National Security Archive, Electronic Briefing Book No. 437, Document 7

stops.name: Cementerio General, Santiago, the funeral held seventeen years late
stops.date_confidence: Attested by es.wikipedia's 'Fundacion Salvador Allende': the final obsequies were held on 4 September 1990 and the Mausoleo Salvador Allende was created at the Cementerio General de Santiago, the date chosen because it was the traditional Chilean presidential polling day. Coordinates are an approximate placement near the southern part of the cemetery, not a verified plot.
stops.campa: Democracy comes back and the country digs him up out of another family's tomb and buries him properly, in Santiago, with a head of state's honours and a crowd along the whole route. The date is chosen deliberately: the fourth of September, the day Chileans used to elect presidents, the day he won in 1970. His widow, home from twenty years of exile, walks behind the coffin. In 2000 a statue of him will be set up facing the palace, arms at his sides, and the arguments will start again about whether that is the man.
stops.quote: History is ours, and people make history.
stops.quote_source: Salvador Allende, 'Last Words to the Nation', Radio Magallanes, Santiago, 11 September 1973, trans. Yoshie Furuhashi (Marxists Internet Archive)
suggested_refs: The Mausoleo Salvador Allende, Cementerio General de Santiago
Arturo Hevia's statue of Allende, Plaza de la Constitucion, unveiled 26 June 2000

stops.name: Cementerio General, Santiago, the exhumation
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the year and the finding: a court ordered the exhumation in May 2011, a Chilean television report on 31 May 2011 revealed a 300-page secret military account and two forensic experts initially suggested assassination, and in July 2011 the international panel concluded death by self-inflicted gunshot from a rifle set to automatic fire. The exact day of the exhumation was not confirmed and the stop is dated to the July finding.
stops.campa: A judge orders the grave opened. An international forensic team takes the remains apart, measures the wound track, models the weapon, and reports that the injuries are those of a man who shot himself under the chin with an automatic rifle, exactly as the physician in the doorway said in 1973. The family, who never disputed it, accept the finding. The court closes the case and he is put back in the mausoleum. The finding is dated July 2011; the day the grave was actually opened is not recorded anywhere reached.
suggested_refs: The 2011 international forensic report on the remains of Salvador Allende
